questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Argue the strongest case for a single language of official records
questions.stem: In a clinic note, a clinician writes that records must be kept in the state language only, with occasional informal translation for patients who ask. Which argument most strongly supports that rule?

options.text: A single official record keeps clinical findings comparable and prevents transcription errors
Patients who speak another language can rely on relatives to explain the notes to them
options.misconception: assumes informal help substitutes for the record

options.text: Clinicians find it easier to consult with colleagues when everyone uses one language
options.misconception: prioritises staff convenience over record integrity

options.text: Translation services are expensive and state hospitals should not carry that cost
options.misconception: treats cost as a sufficient reason to withhold access

questions.explanation: A single official language makes the record comparable across clinics and removes the risk that meaning shifts in translation. Convenience for staff, family help and cost are arguments about administration rather than about the quality of the record itself.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a state adopts national symbols that divide some citizens
questions.stem: A clinic records that patients respond to the national anthem differently from the way they respond to the flag. Explain why a state may adopt national symbols even when they divide citizens.

answer.exemplar: Symbols perform work that arguments cannot. A flag or an anthem compresses a long, contested story into something that can be shown at a ceremony, worn on a uniform or printed on a document, and it does this without requiring the holder to be able to explain it. That is why a state adopts symbols even when sections of the population find them alien: the purpose is not only to include everyone but to give the polity something that can be recognised instantly, which is what makes public space legible and collective feeling operable. The cost is real. A symbol that is only ever experienced as belonging to one group of citizens becomes a marker of who counts, and clinics see the consequences in the form of patients who avoid ceremonies, hide their backgrounds or feel unwelcome in public institutions. The design question is therefore not whether to have symbols but how they are made: symbols that are recognisably national, that are used in ordinary services rather than only in moments of ceremony, and that are explained rather than left as unargued assertions, can carry more people than symbols that are defended with force.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that symbols make a polity legible and recognisable at low cost, while acknowledging the exclusion they cause and linking that to how the symbols are used and explained.
questions.hint: Ask what a symbol does that an argument cannot.

questions.stem: A border survey asked 160 patients whether they felt strongly, moderately or not at all attached to their area: 40 felt strongly, 64 moderately and 56 not at all. What percentage felt at least moderately attached?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the step that turned a language dispute into a breakdown

stimulus.body: Two districts with different official languages disputed the siting of a regional hospital. The dispute ran for eleven months, during which each district's health authority issued letters restating its own position. questions.stem: On the evidence of the note, which factor most likely drove the dispute from disagreement to breakdown?

options.text: The hospital site affects the income of practitioners in each district
options.misconception: invents an economic stake the note does not record

options.text: Each side repeated its own case without the direct meeting that could test it
The two languages make the original documents unreadable to each side
options.misconception: assumes a translation barrier the note does not report

options.text: The national government has not yet chosen between the two districts
options.misconception: invents a third-party decision the note does not mention

questions.explanation: The note records eleven months of parallel statements, four declined meetings and no joint discussion, so the dispute escalated because the claims were never tested against each other directly. The other readings introduce interests, barriers or decisions the note does not mention.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish integration from assimilation in the experience of patients
questions.stem: A clinician asks why a policy described as integration is sometimes experienced by patients as pressure to give up their own language. Explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: Integration and assimilation are easily confused because both are offered in the same language of welcome, but they point in different directions. Integration describes what happens between groups: members of a minority are expected to take part in the institutions of the state, and the state is expected in return to open those institutions to them. Assimilation describes an expectation about the person: the minority is expected to become like the majority, to give up the language, the diet, the celebration or the religious practice that marked it out. A policy can therefore be genuinely integrative in its institutions while still carrying an assimilative expectation in its daily practice, and patients report the second even when the first is in place. The clinical consequences follow from that gap. A patient who is treated well but warned not to use the family language, or advised to avoid a name that marks the family out, learns that safety and belonging depend on becoming less visibly different. Practices that keep the demand for change on the institutions rather than on the patient, such as interpreting, translated records and public use of minority languages, make integration a reciprocal bargain.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should distinguish integration as mutual participation in shared institutions from assimilation as an expectation that the minority become like the majority, and connect that gap to how patients experience the policy.
questions.hint: Ask whether change is demanded of institutions or people.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a curriculum carries a narrative into adult life
questions.stem: Patients who studied the national history curriculum at school often describe their country in terms of its founding stories. Explain why a curriculum can carry a narrative into adult life.

answer.exemplar: A curriculum does not only transmit information; it supplies the categories people later use when they explain the world to themselves and to their children. The national history taught at school does two things. It fixes a sequence, deciding which events are treated as beginnings, turning points and consequences, and it fixes an interpretation, deciding which actors are central and which are background. Both survive long after the lessons end, because they are not stored as facts but as a template. A patient who was taught that the state was founded by a heroic struggle will reach for that frame to explain a contemporary problem, and will read a group's claims in terms of loyalty to that founding. Clinicians should recognise how much such a narrative shapes what counts as normal and who is expected to prove their attachment, and should note the cost where the curriculum was written from a single perspective: the groups whose experience was rendered background have no shared vocabulary with it, and so find themselves outside the story that everyone else is telling.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that curriculum fixes both a sequence and an interpretation, that these persist as a template people reuse, and that a single-perspective curriculum leaves some groups outside the shared story.
questions.hint: Ask what the curriculum makes easy to remember.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risks in reading census identity categories
questions.stem: A clinician asks how a census question that offers separate boxes for language, ethnicity and religion can end up misleading a reader. Explain the risk.

answer.exemplar: A census cannot report the complexity of identity, so it breaks it into boxes, and readers quickly treat the boxes as the thing itself. The risk is not that the boxes are inaccurate but that they become the basis for decisions while the categories they imply are treated as fixed and mutually exclusive. A respondent who speaks a minority language and belongs to an ethnic group and follows a religion has been recorded three times over, and the multiplication of the boxes can produce a picture of the population in which certain combinations look more numerous than they are, because the categories overlap unevenly across the population. A second risk is that a question with no option for a mixed or changing answer forces people into the nearest fit, and the resulting figures then appear to describe people more firmly than the respondents themselves would. The practical lesson for anyone using census data is to treat the categories as one administrative device among several, to check the notes for how refusals and multiple responses were handled, and to read them alongside other sources rather than as a map of who people are.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that the boxes are an administrative device, that overlapping categories can produce misleading counts and forced choices, and that the notes on refusals and multiple answers must be read.
questions.hint: Ask what a forced choice does to the figures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why civic definitions leave room for ethnic accounts
questions.stem: A state that defines membership in civic terms still struggles when communities describe themselves in ethnic ones. Explain the difficulty.

answer.exemplar: A civic definition of membership says that people belong because they hold a legal status and accept the institutions that go with it, and it is attractive because it is universal and because it does not privilege anyone by descent. Its weakness is that it answers the question of who is a member but not the question of what the state is for, and people fill that second gap with an account of the state's history, its religion, its language or its founding people. When communities describe themselves in ethnic terms, they are usually not denying civic membership; they are naming a different thing, namely a shared origin that the state has not itself articulated. The friction comes when the state expects the second question to be answered in the first vocabulary. Clinicians see the result in the gap between the legal status a patient holds and the belonging the patient feels, and in the hesitation of people who can prove the first but cannot find the second anywhere in the public life of the state. A state that can say what it is for in language that does not require descent has a better chance of making civic membership mean something to everyone.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that civic membership answers who belongs but not what the state is for, that people fill that gap with shared-origin accounts, and that a state which states its purpose in non-hereditary terms fares better.
questions.hint: Ask what a civic definition leaves unanswered.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a difference in cross-border service use
questions.stem: A study of two border districts found that in the first, 62 per cent of patients travelled to the neighbouring district for secondary care, while in the second the figure was 9 per cent. Which difference best explains the pattern?

options.text: The second district has better hospitals than its neighbour
options.misconception: assumes quality explains cross-border travel

options.text: The second district's patients are less willing to cross administrative lines
options.misconception: attributes the pattern to patient attitudes without evidence

options.text: The first district's services cross the border while the second's do not
The second district's roads make crossing the border impractical
options.misconception: invents a transport barrier the record does not mention

questions.explanation: Cross-border use of this kind normally reflects the location of services rather than the preferences of patients, and a figure of 62 per cent against 9 per cent is too large a gap for attitude alone to explain. The other readings assume quality, attitudes or transport barriers that the record does not supply.
questions.hint: Ask where the services are located.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why interpreting alone does not secure equal access
questions.stem: A clinician asks why providing an interpreter at the consultation but keeping records only in the state language leaves patients less able to manage their own health. Explain the problem.

answer.exemplar: An interpreter makes the conversation work, but health care does not consist only of conversations. Patients have to read letters, understand test results, judge symptoms, take medication correctly and decide when to return, and all of that happens through the written record and the patient's own knowledge of it. If the record is only in a language the patient reads poorly, the interpreter is present for one of the two channels through which care is delivered and absent for the other. The patient is then dependent on whoever reads the letters for them, which may be a family member with no medical training, and may simply avoid asking for a copy at all, because asking reveals a dependence they would rather hide. The result is a set of practical losses: medication taken wrongly, warning letters not acted on, appointments missed, and a growing reluctance to engage with services. Making provision means translation of the record, not only of the encounter, and it also means telling patients in their own language what has been written about them and what they are expected to do next.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should show that care runs through both conversation and the written record, that written-only provision leaves patients dependent on others, and that the loss is practical as well as symbolic.
questions.hint: Ask what happens between consultations.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of people using a minority language
questions.stem: In a census of 500 people, 210 selected only the state language, 120 only a minority language and 170 a mixture. What percentage of people used a minority language to some degree?
questions.explanation: The 120 who use only a minority language plus the 170 who use both make 290, and 290 out of 500 is 58 per cent. The tempting figure of 42 uses the 210 who use only the state language, which is the complement of the figure asked for.
questions.hint: Add the two groups that use a minority language.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the change that removes a barrier to service uptake

stimulus.body: The review examined why uptake of antenatal classes was lower among women who had recently arrived. It found that class materials were printed only in the state language, that attendance dropped sharply when a class was moved to a venue used by another community, and that among women who did attend, satisfaction was high and several had asked for classes in their own language.

questions.stem: According to the review, which change would most improve uptake?

options.text: Send each woman a reminder letter in the state language before her appointment
options.misconception: assumes attendance turns on reminders rather than on the class

options.text: Provide the classes in the languages the women attending them use
Hold the classes in larger halls so that more women can attend at once
options.misconception: addresses capacity rather than the language barrier

options.text: Publicise the classes more widely across the whole district
options.misconception: increases exposure without removing the obstacle

questions.explanation: The review links low uptake to the language of the materials and to a venue associated with another community, while satisfaction among those who attended was high and requests for classes in other languages were made, so provision in those languages addresses the obstacle directly. Reminders, bigger halls and wider publicity leave that obstacle in place.
questions.hint: Ask what the dissatisfied and satisfied groups said.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a public language and a household language serve different purposes
questions.stem: A health ministry may insist that its language be the language of official business while accepting that some citizens will not use it at home. Explain the apparent inconsistency.

answer.exemplar: There is no inconsistency once the two purposes are separated. The state's language serves as a public language: it is the medium in which laws are written, records are kept, courts conduct business and services are coordinated across a whole territory, and for those purposes a shared medium is what makes the state legible to itself and to its citizens. The household language serves private and community life, in which the state has no business and in which the variety of the population is a resource rather than a problem. The difficulty arises where the two are allowed to blur, as when the official language is treated as a marker of who properly belongs, or when an official is expected to use it in places where its use makes other people feel excluded. Clinicians meet the result in patients who decline to engage in the official language even where they can, because the language of institutions has become associated with judgement of them. A state that treats its language as the language of business and of shared public life, and leaves the household to its own arrangements, avoids making the second a test of belonging.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should separate the state's language as a shared medium of public business from the household languages of private life, and explain how blurring the two turns the official language into a test of belonging.
questions.hint: Ask what each language is for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how studying a community as an actor changes interpretation

stimulus.body: A school note records that pupils in the upper secondary history course who had taken the optional local history module wrote longer and more specific accounts of local disputes than those who had not. A colleague observed that the module covered events, including several contested ones, in which the local community appeared as a party rather than as an object of state policy.

questions.stem: What explains the difference between the two groups in the note?

options.text: Studying the community as a participant supplies a repertoire for interpreting later disputes
The optional module attracted pupils who were already more interested in local affairs
options.misconception: treats selection into the module as the whole explanation

options.text: Pupils who took more history lessons wrote longer answers
options.misconception: reduces the effect to the sheer volume of history teaching

options.text: The contested events in the module discouraged pupils from writing about them
options.misconception: predicts the opposite of what was observed

questions.explanation: The note links the difference to the way the module treated the community, as a party with its own conduct, which supplies a frame for reading later disputes, and the colleague's observation supports that reading. Selection effects, lesson volume and discouragement are not evidenced by the note.
questions.hint: Ask what the module did differently.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why some symbols attract more attachment than others
questions.stem: A clinician notes that patients speak of the national flag with warmth, of the anthem with indifference and of the state emblem with irritation. What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: The flag is the object of real feeling while the others are administrative necessities
options.misconception: reads indifference as approval and irritation as rationality

options.text: Symbols that carry ceremony attract more attachment than administrative ones
The state has failed to communicate the meaning of its emblem
options.misconception: assumes a communication failure rather than a difference in use

options.text: Patients are critical of national symbols in general
options.misconception: ignores the warm response to the flag

questions.explanation: The flag is the symbol patients encounter in ordinary and affective settings, while the emblem is largely administrative, so the pattern reflects where each is used rather than hostility to the state. The other readings convert indifference into approval, assume a communication failure, or overlook the warm response to the flag.
questions.hint: Ask where each symbol is normally encountered.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the effect of a border drawn without regard to communities
questions.stem: A region's current administrative line was drawn in a century ago by a colonial administration with no regard for existing communities. Which statement best describes the result?

options.text: The communities inside the border have accepted the new arrangement without exception
options.misconception: claims acceptance that the record of divided communities contradicts

options.text: The border has no practical effect because communities ignore it in practice
options.misconception: overstates the practical irrelevance of the border

options.text: The border divides communities whose economic and social life still crosses it
The communities concerned would be better served by returning to the old arrangement
options.misconception: presumes the earlier arrangement could simply be restored

questions.explanation: A boundary drawn without regard to existing communities leaves those communities split while their economic and social life continues across the line, which is why cross-border use persists. The other readings claim universal acceptance, deny the border's practical effects or assume the earlier arrangement could be restored.
questions.hint: Ask what the communities continued to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one dispute settles quickly and another does not
questions.stem: A review of two regional disputes found that the first was settled in four months and the second took two years. The first was resolved by a joint commission; the second involved repeated parallel statements and a third party that rejected both positions. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The first dispute concerned a less important subject than the second
options.misconception: assumes importance explains the duration without evidence

options.text: The second dispute had a larger population in one of the communities
options.misconception: invents a demographic cause the review does not record

options.text: The second dispute was in a region with a longer history of language conflict
options.misconception: supplies a historical cause the review does not mention

options.text: A process the parties could accept settled the first dispute

questions.explanation: The first dispute ended quickly under a joint commission the parties accepted, while the second dragged on because both positions were repeated and the third party rejected both, so no acceptable way of deciding existed. The other readings supply causes the review does not record.
questions.hint: Compare the ways the two disputes were decided.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a colonial border affects ties that cross it
questions.stem: Families separated by a colonial border often keep sending relatives and money across it for three generations. Explain what the border did to those ties.

answer.exemplar: The border did not create the ties; it interrupted them. The family before the line was drawn traded, married, worshipped and settled disputes along the same routes, and those routes continued to function afterwards because they rested on obligation rather than on jurisdiction. Crossing the line in order to maintain a relationship therefore became an act with a legal risk attached to it, and a risk that was constant and invisible to those outside the community. Two things then happened that make the pattern durable. First, the family built a habit of moving people and resources across the line, and habit is what later generations inherit along with the story of why it was necessary. Second, the very fact that the crossing requires effort is what keeps the tie strong, because a relationship that costs something to maintain is treated as one worth maintaining, and because the effort itself becomes part of the family's account of who it is. Clinicians meeting patients whose family histories run along such lines should recognise the crossing as evidence of durable obligation rather than as irregularity, and should expect that the obligations of the other side of the line will continue to shape how the family makes decisions here.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that the border interrupted existing ties rather than creating them, and that the cost and habit of crossing is what has kept those obligations alive across generations.
questions.hint: Ask what the border interrupted rather than created.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the risk created by separately published census tables

stimulus.body: The census asked respondents to record their main language, and to tick every additional language spoken. The note records that 62 per cent of respondents ticked at least one additional language, that 9 per cent declined the question entirely, and that in the published tables the main language and the additional languages are shown in separate tables.

questions.stem: What risk does a reader of the published tables face, given the note?

options.text: The tables will overstate the number of people who speak only the state language
options.misconception: assumes overlap is counted twice across the tables

options.text: The tables will show that most people prefer their home language
options.misconception: infers preference from a record of languages used

options.text: The tables hide how many people use more than one language
The tables will understate the number who declined to answer
options.misconception: ignores the stated refusal rate

questions.explanation: Because main and additional languages are shown separately, a reader looking at only the main-language table will miss the 62 per cent who use more than one language, and the two tables cannot be combined without the overlap being handled. The other readings misstate the effect, infer preference, or ignore a stated rate.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader sees in only one of the tables.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret acceptance of services without acceptance of ceremony
questions.stem: A clinician observes that minority patients accept the state's health services but avoid its ceremonies. Which reading fits this pattern best?

options.text: The state has been accepted as a provider but not yet as a possessor to celebrate
The patients are using the services but refusing to acknowledge the state
options.misconception: reads service use as a form of defiance

options.text: The services themselves are of such poor quality that only the ceremonies are rejected
options.misconception: invents poor quality that the pattern does not show

options.text: The patients are simply less interested in public events than other groups
options.misconception: generalises from a group without comparison

questions.explanation: Using public services while declining public ritual suggests that the state is accepted as an institution that provides but not yet as something to feel part of, which is a common transitional pattern. questions.explanation: The difference between 90 who chose the state language and 46 who chose their home language is 44 patients. The tempting figure of 26 compares the home-language group with the group choosing both, which answers a different question.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Draw an inference about civic belonging from a change in participation

stimulus.body: A community note records that the town's annual day was reorganised so that contributions from each ethnic community were presented in a shared programme, and that the note attributes the change to a petition organised by two of the communities. It also records that the number of participating organisations rose from four to eleven, while the number of organisations that withdrew in protest fell from three to none.

questions.stem: What does the reorganisation described in the note suggest about civic belonging?

options.text: The town's official day had previously been organised without any minority input
options.misconception: claims an absence that the note does not describe

options.text: Participation rose when the communities were able to shape the shared event
The number of participating organisations matters more than who organises the day
options.misconception: reads the count as sufficient without regard to who arranged it

options.text: Protest by withdrawing organisations is a legitimate way to claim recognition
options.misconception: treats withdrawal as the successful route rather than the failing one

questions.explanation: The note attributes the change to a petition and links it to a rise in participation and the disappearance of withdrawals, which suggests that the communities' standing depends on shaping the event rather than withdrawing from it. The other readings assert an absence, ignore who arranged it, or treat withdrawal as success.
questions.hint: Compare what changed when the organisers changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a single-perspective curriculum on minority students
questions.stem: A patient who was taught a history curriculum presenting one group as the origin of the nation struggles to explain their own community's place in it. What does this suggest?

options.text: A curriculum written from one viewpoint leaves some groups without a place in the story
The patient has not studied the curriculum carefully enough
options.misconception: blames the patient's attention rather than the curriculum

options.text: Curricula should be left entirely to local communities to write
options.misconception: prescribes decentralisation rather than examining the narrative

options.text: Students should be taught to memorise minority accounts alongside the national one
options.misconception: proposes a content fix that misses the framing problem

questions.explanation: If the narrative is written from a single viewpoint, the groups it treats as background inherit no vocabulary for describing themselves, and the difficulty the patient reports is a property of the curriculum rather than of the student's effort. questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose the criterion that governs symbol display in public institutions
questions.stem: A clinic is asked to display a national emblem and the state flag in its waiting room. Which arrangement best reflects what symbols are for?

options.text: Display whichever symbol staff and patients have expressed most interest in
options.misconception: makes popularity rather than function the criterion

options.text: Display the symbols that the state uses to identify its public institutions
Display the symbols that members of each community consider their own
options.misconception: treats the room as a place for competing claims

options.text: Display no symbols, since patients may react badly to any of them
options.misconception: avoids the question of what public institutions represent

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a belonging distribution after a border change
questions.stem: A survey found that 240 patients were asked which region they felt part of: 108 named their region of residence, 72 an ancestral region, 40 the state and 20 none. What does the distribution support?

options.text: Nearly half of the patients rejected their region of residence
options.misconception: misreads the ancestral group as rejection of residence

options.text: The state is the most common object of belonging
options.misconception: ignores the much larger residence group

options.text: Most patients name the region they live in, and a large minority name an ancestral one
Ancestral belonging is displacing residence-based belonging
options.misconception: claims a displacement the counts do not show

questions.explanation: The 108 who named their region of residence are the largest group, while the 72 naming an ancestral region are a large minority alongside 40 who named the state, so most patients locate themselves at home and many locate themselves further back. questions.hint: Identify the largest group before judging.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why language disputes harden as they continue
questions.stem: A dispute over a language requirement often becomes harder to settle the longer it runs. Explain the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: Disputes harden because each side's position becomes tied to what has already been conceded, invested and said in public. Early on, the disagreement is about the substance: which language, where, for whom. As the dispute runs, each side acquires a constituency whose standing depends on the outcome, and the question becomes whether the other side can be made to back down without losing face in front of that constituency. The original substance is then embedded in the grievance and in the precedent, so a compromise that would have been acceptable at the outset is now read as a humiliation. Third parties enter late and find that any settlement must also settle the question of who has the right to decide, which is the part both sides find hardest to concede. Clinicians see the residue of this in patients whose dealings with the state have become procedural and defensive rather than ordinary. The practical lesson is about timing rather than substance: disputes over a language requirement are usually cheap to settle while they are still administrative questions and very expensive once they have become questions of national standing, so a forum that agrees in advance to settle on procedure rather than on principle can often resolve them before the hardening takes place.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that positions become tied to concessions, constituencies and public statements over time, so a late compromise is read as humiliation and the question of who decides becomes the real dispute.
questions.hint: Ask what the passage of time adds to the dispute.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the reach of a request-based translation system

stimulus.body: The note records that the clinic translated letters on request only when the patient asked in person at the desk, that 31 of the 40 translation requests in the year were made by patients who had been told to ask, and that two patients who had received letters in a language they did not read did not attend their next appointment.

questions.stem: What does the request-based system achieve, on the evidence of the note?

options.text: It keeps translation demand low enough for the clinic to manage easily
options.misconception: treats a low request count as evidence of low need

options.text: It identifies the patients who most need translated letters
options.misconception: assumes the requests capture need rather than the reverse

options.text: It ensures that no patient receives a letter they cannot read
options.misconception: ignores the two patients who did

options.text: It reaches only the patients who know to ask for translation

questions.explanation: Thirty-one of the forty requests came from patients who had been told to ask, and two patients received unreadable letters and then missed appointments, so the system selects for the confident and informed rather than for those with the greatest need. The other readings treat low demand as evidence of low need, assume the requests capture need, or overlook the two failures recorded.
questions.hint: Ask who is left outside a request-based system.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a fixed category design contributes to census figures
questions.stem: A clinician reads that a census offers separate categories for language, ethnicity and religion and finds no option for a respondent who changes or combines them. What follows from that design?

options.text: The published categories will describe an administrative choice rather than the population itself
The counts will be biased towards the largest ethnic group in the area
options.misconception: invents a bias that the design does not produce

options.text: The census should be abandoned in favour of local consultation
options.misconception: prescribes abandoning a method rather than reading it

options.text: No useful information can be drawn from census identity data at all
options.misconception: dismisses the data rather than interpreting it carefully

questions.explanation: When a questionnaire offers only separate, fixed categories, what the figures describe is the shape of the instrument as much as the shape of the population, so the categories must be read as an administrative choice. questions.hint: Ask what the instrument itself contributes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the problem with making a language a condition of care
questions.stem: A health service introduces a programme requiring patients to attend information sessions in the state language before receiving a course of treatment. Which criticism best describes the problem with it?

options.text: The sessions cost money that could be spent on treatment itself
options.misconception: focuses on cost rather than on the condition attached

options.text: It makes the patient's own language a condition of getting care
The sessions are too long to fit into the appointment schedule
options.misconception: raises a scheduling point rather than the substantive one

options.text: Clinicians are not trained to run sessions in the state language
options.misconception: locates the barrier in staff capability rather than in the rule

questions.explanation: Requiring a session in the state language before treatment makes the patient's own language a condition of receiving care, which is the assimilation pattern rather than integration, since the demand for change falls on the patient rather than on the service. The other readings raise costs, scheduling and training points that do not address the condition attached.
questions.hint: Ask who has to change for the care to proceed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the risk created by slow translation of official guidance

stimulus.body: The ministry's note records that clinical guidelines are issued only in the state language, that a translation of one guideline took eleven months to complete, and that during that period regional services reported acting on locally improvised versions of the guidance. The note also records that no procedure exists for deciding which guidelines should be translated first.

questions.stem: What problem does the translation delay create, according to the note?

options.text: Clinicians ignore guidance written in a language they read less fluently
options.misconception: assumes a general reading difficulty the note does not report

options.text: The ministry should simply publish all guidance in every language
options.misconception: prescribes a costly answer without addressing prioritisation

options.text: Clinicians act on improvised guidance while the official version is unavailable
Translation is unnecessary because clinical practice does not vary by region
options.misconception: denies the variation that improvised versions respond to

questions.explanation: The note records that services improvised their own guidance during the eleven-month delay, so the risk is divergence from official practice while the official version is unavailable. The other readings assert a reading difficulty, prescribe universal translation without solving prioritisation, or deny that practice varies.
questions.hint: Ask what services did while they waited.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain two different vocabularies of belonging
questions.stem: A clinician notes that one community describes itself in terms of shared origin while another describes itself in terms of shared institutions. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: The two communities ground their belonging in different kinds of thing
The first community has not accepted the state's institutions
options.misconception: infers refusal to accept from a different description

options.text: The second community is more assimilated than the first
options.misconception: ranks the two descriptions as degrees of assimilation

options.text: One of the two descriptions must be mistaken for the other
options.misconception: assumes the two styles compete for the same ground

questions.hint: Ask what each description takes as its ground.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the message pupils take from a choice of sources
questions.stem: A curriculum review finds that lessons on the founding period are taught from a single official text while lessons on recent events use several competing accounts. Which effect is most likely?

options.text: Pupils learn that recent history is contested and the founding period is settled
options.misconception: assumes the official text persuades rather than instructs

options.text: Pupils are taught to treat the founding period as settled and recent events as open
Pupils conclude that only recent history is worth debating
options.misconception: infers a preference the curriculum does not convey

options.text: Pupils cannot compare the two periods because the methods differ
options.misconception: describes an inconsistency rather than an implied claim

questions.explanation: Using a single official account for the founding period and competing accounts for recent events tells pupils which questions are closed and which are open, so the apparently even-handed teaching of recent history is itself a claim. The other readings assume persuasion, infer a preference or describe a methodological inconsistency.
questions.hint: Ask what the choice of sources implies to pupils.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a distribution of acceptance of public symbols
questions.stem: Among 300 patients asked which of three symbols they would be content to see in a public waiting room, 120 named the flag, 90 the emblem, 60 the anthem, and 30 would accept none of them. What does the distribution show?

options.text: Contentment with the flag is much lower than for the other two symbols
options.misconception: reverses the comparison the figures show

options.text: Most patients accept at least one of the three symbols
options.misconception: treats the 270 who named one as if it were a majority of all

options.text: A minority of patients would accept none of the symbols in a public room
The emblem is the most widely accepted symbol
options.misconception: ignores the larger flag group

questions.explanation: Thirty of the 300 patients would accept none of the three, which is a minority of ten per cent, while the remaining 270 named one they would be content to see. The other readings reverse the comparison, treat a large majority as a majority, or overlook the larger flag group.
questions.hint: Compare the none group with the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a colonial map shapes later feelings of belonging
questions.stem: A map drawn under colonial rule can still shape where people feel they belong a century later. Explain the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: The map continues to shape feeling because belonging is not only a matter of opinion; it is formed by the institutions through which a person is recognised and deals. A border drawn without regard to settlement created administrative units that were then given their own courts, schools, clinics and markets, and those institutions recruited loyalties which were themselves shaped by the unit in which a family found itself. The identities that grew up around those institutions were not chosen in a vacuum; they were produced by the arrangement the border installed, and they have been reproduced ever since through schooling, work, marriage and the allocation of services. There is also an institutional afterlife. Where the map is still the basis on which representation is allocated, public investment is distributed and identity documents are issued, the map remains the operative reality, and feeling follows the institutions that continue to administer people. Clinicians should therefore treat contested local identities as a durable consequence of institutional history rather than as a passing sentiment, and should expect that a change in the map without a change in the institutions would reproduce the same pattern under a new outline.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should explain that the border created institutions which then produced the loyalties, and that feeling persists because the map continues to govern representation, services and recognition.
questions.hint: Ask what the map did after it was drawn.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the average of two competing boundary positions
questions.stem: Two neighbouring districts disputed the position of a language boundary. A commission proposed 120 kilometres, the first district argued for 180 and the second for 90. What was the average of the two districts' positions, in kilometres?
questions.explanation: The average of 180 and 90 kilometres is 135, which is also where the commission's proposal of 120 sits between the two claims. The tempting figure of 150 uses the commission's proposal instead of the mean of the two positions.
questions.hint: Add the two positions and divide by two.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a legal arrangement against continuing everyday practice

stimulus.body: The note records that a village divided by the colonial boundary holds two sets of registers, one for each side, and that residents travel to the village on the other side for baptisms, funerals and the weekly market. It also records that since the boundary was redrawn administratively without altering the road network, 78 per cent of local journeys still crossed it.

questions.stem: What does the register arrangement in the note show?

options.text: The boundary is a legal line that everyday practice continues to ignore
The two sides have developed entirely separate legal identities
options.misconception: overstates the separation that the shared journeys contradict

options.text: The road network was built after the boundary was drawn
options.misconception: reverses the sequence the note records

options.text: Residents on the two sides no longer recognise each other
options.misconception: contradicts the shared ceremonies the note describes

questions.explanation: Keeping separate registers shows that the boundary has legal force, while the journeys, ceremonies and markets that continue to cross it show that it has not replaced the older pattern of life. The other readings overstate the separation, reverse the sequence of road and boundary, or contradict the shared ceremonies recorded.
questions.hint: Compare the registers with the journeys.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose the provision that closes a gap across service channels
questions.stem: A clinic reviews its approach to patients who speak a minority language and finds that interpreters are used in consultations but not in telephone appointments. Which change closes the gap?

options.text: Ask patients to bring a relative who can interpret on the telephone
options.misconception: relies on unpaid support instead of provision

options.text: Provide interpreting for telephone appointments as well as for consultations
Replace telephone appointments with written messages in the state language
options.misconception: switches the channel instead of removing the language barrier

options.text: Limit telephone appointments to patients who can use the state language
options.misconception: excludes the patients the provision exists for

questions.explanation: A patient who cannot follow a telephone conversation in the state language faces the same barrier in that channel as in the clinic room, so interpreting has to cover both. Unpaid relatives, written messages and restricting appointments each leave the barrier or exclude the patient rather than remove it.
questions.hint: Ask which channels the barrier runs through.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select the most suitable source for estimating minority language use
questions.stem: A clinician needs to estimate how many patients in a clinic catchment use a minority language at home. Which source of information is most suitable?

options.text: The proportion of the district's population that was born abroad
options.misconception: uses nationality of birth as a proxy for language use

options.text: The number of patients who have asked for an interpreter in the past year
options.misconception: counts only the requests that reached the desk

options.text: Census counts of main and additional languages for the same catchment area
The proportion of households in the area that receive translated post
options.misconception: infers language from a downstream service use

questions.explanation: Census tables record how many people use each language, including the additional languages that a single-question count would miss, and cover the whole population of the catchment rather than only those who came forward. The other sources are proxies that understate or misidentify the group.
questions.hint: Ask which source counts languages across a whole population.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a redesign of service delivery reveals about barriers
questions.stem: A review found that minority patients' use of preventive services rose to near the national rate once the services were redesigned around their own community's health workers. What does this suggest?

options.text: Preventive services are inherently unpopular with minority patients
options.misconception: attributes a barrier that the redesign removed

options.text: The national rate was set too high for minority communities
options.misconception: blames the target rather than the delivery

options.text: Community health workers are more effective than professional staff in every case
options.misconception: generalises far beyond what the review shows

options.text: The barrier was how the service was delivered rather than the service itself

questions.explanation: The rate rose when delivery was redesigned around the community's own workers, which points to accessibility and trust in the delivery as the barrier rather than to the value of prevention. The other readings treat the service as unpopular, blame the target or generalise the result beyond its scope.
questions.hint: Ask what changed when the rate rose.
